name: Dextroamphetamine/Amphetamine (Adderall, Adderall XR, Mydayis)
summary: Prescription stimulant used for ADHD (and IR Adderall for narcolepsy). Helps with focus and impulse control, but can worsen anxiety, appetite, and sleep—plus it carries real misuse/addiction and cardiovascular risks.
description: Adderall-type stimulants can seriously improve attention, follow-through, and daytime functioning. They can also crank up insomnia, appetite loss, jitteriness, and irritability—especially if the dose is too high or timing is off. This medication is a Schedule II controlled substance for a reason: misuse can lead to overdose and death. If you have a history of substance use, bipolar disorder, psychosis, tics, or heart disease, your prescriber should treat that as a big deal and plan monitoring accordingly.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: CNS Stimulant (Amphetamine Mixed Salts; Immediate- and Extended-Release Formulations)

linked_conditions.context: Stimulants are a first-line option for ADHD. The goal is not to make you feel 'wired'—it’s to improve attention, task initiation, impulse control, and follow-through with the lowest effective dose.

Immediate-release mixed amphetamine salts are FDA-approved for narcolepsy-related daytime sleepiness. Extended-release use for narcolepsy is sometimes used off-label after a stable effective dose is found.

Some clinicians use extended-release amphetamine as an alternative agent in cocaine use disorder (sometimes alongside topiramate). This is off-label and requires careful risk-benefit thinking, especially around misuse risk.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to amphetamine or any component of the formulation (eg, angioedema, anaphylaxis)
Use during or within 14 days of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs), including linezolid or IV methylene blue

efficacy_response.comparison_data: Stimulants consistently outperform placebo in controlled trials
efficacy_response.patient_text: When stimulants work, the change is usually obvious: less mental static, better follow-through, fewer impulsive detours, and fewer 'I know what to do, I just can’t start' moments. If you feel only side effects with no functional benefit, that’s a dosing/timing/problem-to-solve—not a reason to just push higher.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral absorption with formulation-dependent release patterns
pharmacokinetics.onset: Often felt the same day; timing depends on IR vs ER
pharmacokinetics.time_to_peak: Immediate release ~3 hours; Adderall XR ~7 hours; Mydayis ~8 hours (and can be later in some people)
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Adults: d-amphetamine ~10 hours; l-amphetamine ~13 hours (varies by age and individual metabolism)
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic oxidation; CYP2D6 contributes to metabolite formation
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Urine; elimination strongly affected by urinary pH (acidic urine clears faster; alkaline urine clears slower)
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food may delay peak levels for some extended-release products; consistency matters for predictable timing

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Adderall-type mixed amphetamine salts are prescribed to treat {link:condition:attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder:ADHD}—especially when distractibility, impulsivity, and executive dysfunction are wrecking school, work, or relationships. The immediate-release form is also FDA-approved for {link:condition:narcolepsy:narcolepsy} (daytime sleepiness).
items: {link:condition:attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder:ADHD}: Improve attention, task initiation, follow-through, and impulse control
off_label: {link:condition:cocaine-use-disorder:Cocaine use disorder} (alternative agent, typically extended-release; specialist-level monitoring recommended)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Here’s the real-world vibe people report. Not everyone feels all of this, but the patterns are common:

items.category: Focus turns on (when it’s the right dose)
quotes: My brain got quieter. I could actually pick one thing and stay with it.
It didn’t feel like motivation magically appeared—it just stopped feeling impossible to start.
Less bouncing between tabs, less doom-scrolling, more finishing.

items.category: Drive and productivity (sometimes a little too much)
quotes: I got a ton done, but I had to remember to eat and drink water.
I can lock in… and then realize I’ve been hyperfocused for hours.
If I take it late, my sleep is toast.
Food felt optional. I had to schedule meals like a task.
I lost weight without trying—and then my mood got worse because I wasn’t eating.
When it wears off, I get hungry all at once.
items.note: Appetite suppression is one of the most common issues, and it’s more than “annoying” if it affects growth (kids) or mood/anxiety (anyone).

items.category: Jitters, anxiety, and irritability (usually a dosing/timing problem)
quotes: If the dose is too high, I feel tense—like my body is running and my brain is trying to keep up.
I got snappy. Not angry like me—just… less patient.
My heart felt faster and it made me spiral a bit.
items.note: If your anxiety spikes, that’s a signal to adjust dose, formulation, timing, caffeine, sleep, or comorbid anxiety treatment—not to white-knuckle it.

quotes: Around late afternoon I feel flat, tired, and kind of sad for no reason.
When it drops, my ADHD comes back hard and I’m useless for an hour.
I get a headache and want to lie down.
items.note: Crashes can improve with dose adjustments, smoother extended-release coverage, food/hydration, or a carefully planned schedule.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Stimulants aren’t like antidepressants—you don’t wait weeks to know if it’s doing something. Timing depends heavily on the formulation.
key_points: Same day: Many people notice effects the first day (especially with IR)
Mydayis: Can last up to ~16 hours (which is great for coverage, but can be brutal for insomnia if timing is off)
Extended-release timing is less “instant,” more gradual—expect a smoother ramp up and longer tail

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Stimulants are one of the most consistently effective medication classes in psychiatry for ADHD. The point isn’t just symptom scores—it’s whether you can start tasks, finish tasks, regulate attention, and show up more consistently in your real life. If you’re only getting side effects, your plan needs a rethink (dose, timing, formulation, sleep, anxiety, or whether a different medication fits better).
sections.clinical_details: Across controlled trials and meta-analyses, amphetamine formulations show reliable benefits for ADHD symptoms. Benefits are typically noticeable quickly, while side effects (sleep/appetite/irritability) are often dose- and timing-dependent and can be the limiting factor.

citation.authors: Castells X, Blanco-Silvente L, Cunill R
citation.title: Amphetamines for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in adults

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: This is a Schedule II controlled substance. Misuse can cause overdose and death.
sections.black_box: Dextroamphetamine/amphetamine has a high potential for abuse and misuse, which can lead to substance use disorder, including addiction. Misuse and abuse of CNS stimulants can result in overdose and death, and risk increases with higher doses or unapproved methods of administration (like snorting or injection). Prescribers should assess risk before starting and monitor throughout treatment.
other: Kids <6 years: Extended-release stimulants have higher plasma exposure and higher side effect rates than in older kids, including clinically significant weight loss. If a child <6 is on an extended-release stimulant and losing weight or having other adverse reactions, clinicians should consider stopping and/or switching to an alternative (like an immediate-release option).

Cardiovascular risk: Stimulants can raise heart rate and blood pressure. Serious events (MI, stroke, sudden cardiac death) have been reported, especially in people with underlying heart disease or in overdose/misuse.
Psychiatric risk: New or worsening psychosis or mania can occur—even in people without a prior history. Aggression/hostility can also show up.
Serotonin syndrome: Risk increases when combined with serotonergic meds or CYP2D6 inhibitors that raise amphetamine exposure.
Peripheral vasculopathy: Raynaud-like symptoms can happen (cold, painful, color-changing fingers/toes). Severe cases with ulceration have been reported.
Growth and weight: Appetite suppression and weight loss can be significant; growth slowing has been reported with long-term pediatric treatment.
Seizure considerations: Data are mixed, but if seizures occur, stimulants are typically stopped and reassessed.
patient_counseling: Take it early. Late dosing is one of the fastest ways to accidentally create insomnia.
Track appetite and weight. If you’re not eating, your mood and anxiety often pay the price.
Tell your prescriber immediately about chest pain, fainting, severe shortness of breath, or a racing heart that feels abnormal.
If you develop hallucinations, paranoia, or manic symptoms (no sleep + wired + grandiose/impulsive), stop and contact your prescriber urgently.
Lock it up. Don’t share it. Don’t “experiment” with routes of use. That’s how people end up in the ER—or worse.
Avoid dehydration and be cautious with intense exercise if you notice palpitations or dizziness.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: appetite loss, insomnia, headache, dry mouth, and feeling jittery or on-edge. Many side effects are dose-, timing-, and formulation-dependent.
plain_language_list: Stomach upset (nausea, abdominal pain, constipation or diarrhea)

common.patient_note: This is the side effect that sneaks up on people. If you’re skipping meals, your anxiety, mood, and sleep often get worse. For kids, weight and growth need to be treated as core safety outcomes—not an afterthought.

If you’re taking it late or the duration is longer than your day, sleep gets wrecked. Once sleep goes, everything else follows (irritability, anxiety, focus). Timing and formulation matter a lot here.
Often related to dehydration, not eating, or the medication wearing off. Hydration + food + smoother coverage can help.
This usually means the dose is too high, the timing is off, caffeine is stacking, sleep is insufficient, or there’s untreated anxiety underneath. The fix is adjustment—not just pushing through.
Annoying but manageable: water, sugar-free gum, and dental care matter more than people think.
Stimulants can raise heart rate and blood pressure. If it feels intense, scary, or new—don’t ignore it. Dose and medical screening matter.

serious: Cardiovascular events: acute MI, stroke, sudden cardiac death (rare but high-stakes), especially with underlying heart disease or misuse/overdose
Psychosis or mania: hallucinations, paranoia, delusions, manic escalation (can occur at therapeutic doses)
Serotonin syndrome (when combined with serotonergic agents): agitation, sweating, tremor, diarrhea, fever, confusion—medical emergency
Peripheral vasculopathy (Raynaud phenomenon): painful, color-changing digits; rare cases with ulceration/skin breakdown
Severe weight loss or growth suppression in pediatrics (risk is higher for extended-release products in children <6)
Rhabdomyolysis (rare): muscle pain/weakness, dark urine—medical emergency

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Stimulants interact in two main ways: (1) they can dangerously stack stimulation or serotonin effects, and (2) they can be pushed up or down depending on metabolism and urinary pH.

items.with: MAOIs (including linezolid or IV methylene blue)
items.risk: Contraindicated. Risk of dangerously high blood pressure, hyperthermia, and severe reactions.
items.action: Do not use within 14 days of MAOI therapy.

items.with: SSRIs/SNRIs/other serotonergic meds (eg, duloxetine, venlafaxine, sertraline, fluoxetine; also triptans, tramadol, some migraine meds)
items.risk: Higher serotonin syndrome risk, especially with higher doses or multiple serotonergic agents.
items.action: Use with caution. Educate on early warning signs (agitation, sweating, tremor, diarrhea, fever) and seek urgent care if they appear.

items.with: CYP2D6 inhibitors (eg, fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion; some antipsychotics)
items.risk: Can raise amphetamine exposure in some patients, increasing side effects (anxiety, insomnia, HR/BP effects).
items.action: Consider lower starting doses and slower titration; monitor side effects closely.

items.risk: May reduce serum levels and shorten effect in some people.
items.action: If you notice the medication feels weaker when taken with acidic drinks, separate timing and monitor response.

items.with: Urinary alkalinizing agents (eg, sodium bicarbonate) or alkalinizing diets
items.risk: Can slow elimination and increase exposure, potentially increasing side effects.
items.action: Avoid manipulating urinary pH to change stimulant effects. Tell your prescriber about supplements.

items.with: Other stimulants (including high caffeine, nicotine, decongestants like pseudoephedrine)
items.risk: Stacks stimulation: more anxiety, insomnia, palpitations, blood pressure rise.
items.action: Limit caffeine and avoid combining with other stimulants unless your clinician explicitly plans for it.

items.risk: Stimulants can counteract blood pressure-lowering effects.
items.action: Monitor BP/HR; adjust treatment plan if BP rises.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Stimulants don’t have the same seizure-risk withdrawal pattern as benzodiazepines, but stopping abruptly—especially after high doses or long-term daily use—can cause a crash: intense fatigue, low mood, irritability, and sleep changes. If you’re discontinuing, a planned step-down is often smoother.
key_points: Common “crash” symptoms: fatigue, depressed mood, increased appetite, sleepiness, brain fog
Higher risk of a rough landing: higher doses, long duration of daily use, underlying depression or substance use
Typical approach: gradual dose reduction over days to weeks if you’ve been on a steady daily regimen
If stopping is due to serious side effects (psychosis/mania, severe cardiovascular symptoms): the plan may be urgent—follow medical guidance

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Dosing is individualized. Most titration is done weekly, using the lowest dose that improves function without turning you into a sleepless, snack-avoiding stress machine. Extended-release products are not interchangeable mg-for-mg—product-specific dosing matters.

adult.adhd_ir_initial: 5 mg PO once or twice daily (morning; second dose early afternoon if used)
adult.adhd_ir_titration: Increase total daily dose by 5 to 10 mg at intervals of at least 1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.adhd_ir_selected_patients_max: Up to 60 mg/day may be used in selected patients with close monitoring when clinically necessary
adult.adhd_er_initial: 10 to 20 mg PO once daily in the morning
adult.adhd_er_titration: Increase by 10 to 20 mg at intervals of at least 1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.adhd_er_usual_max: 40 mg/day (higher doses increase adverse effect burden)
adult.adhd_er_selected_patients_max: Up to 60 mg/day may be used in selected patients with close monitoring when clinically necessary
adult.triple_bead_er_initial: 12.5 mg PO once daily in the morning
adult.triple_bead_er_titration: Increase by 12.5 mg at intervals of at least 1 week based on response and tolerability
adult.narcolepsy_ir_initial: 10 mg PO once daily in the morning
adult.narcolepsy_ir_titration: Increase by 10 mg weekly until optimal response
adult.narcolepsy_ir_typical_range: 20 to 60 mg/day in 1 to 3 divided doses (avoid late doses to reduce insomnia)
adult.cocaine_use_disorder_er_initial: 10 to 20 mg PO once daily (sometimes combined with topiramate) (off-label)
adult.cocaine_use_disorder_er_titration: Increase by 10 mg weekly based on response and tolerability (off-label)

sections.simple_explanation: Immediate-release (IR) is shorter (often 4-6 hours) and can be dosed 1-3 times/day, while extended-release (XR/ER) is designed for once-daily coverage. Longer coverage can mean fewer ups/downs—but also more insomnia if the medication outlasts your day.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Stimulants require extra caution in pregnancy, breastfeeding, younger children, and anyone with cardiac risk or psychiatric vulnerability (bipolar disorder, psychosis, substance use history).
sections.pregnancy: Human outcome data exist, but there are still meaningful concerns: stimulants can cause vasoconstriction and may reduce placental perfusion. Use during pregnancy may be associated with risks like low birth weight or premature birth, and newborns may show withdrawal-like symptoms (agitation, irritability, feeding issues, excessive drowsiness). Nonpharmacologic options are preferred for mild-to-moderate ADHD during pregnancy. If medication is used, shared decision-making matters: lowest effective dose, simplest regimen, and careful monitoring.
sections.lactation: Amphetamine and dextroamphetamine pass into breast milk. Reported relative infant dose ranges are variable, and manufacturers generally do not recommend breastfeeding due to potential infant risks (blood pressure/heart rate effects, irritability, poor feeding, sleep disruption, growth concerns). If treatment is considered essential, risk-benefit decisions should be individualized with infant monitoring for feeding difficulties, irritability, and insomnia.
sections.pediatrics: Extended-release stimulants: Not recommended for children younger than 6 years because younger kids can have higher plasma exposure and higher rates of adverse reactions, including clinically significant weight loss. If a child <6 is experiencing weight loss or other adverse effects on an extended-release stimulant, clinicians should consider stopping and/or switching to an alternative (like an immediate-release formulation). For all pediatric patients, growth (height/weight), appetite, sleep, and behavior need routine tracking.
sections.geriatrics: Refer to adult dosing but start low and go slow. Older adults may be more sensitive to blood pressure/heart rate effects, insomnia, and appetite/weight changes. Cardiac screening and BP/HR monitoring become especially important.
sections.hepatic: No formal manufacturer dose adjustments are provided, but use caution; reduced elimination can increase exposure and side effects.
sections.renal: Use caution. For certain extended-release products, severe renal impairment requires lower dosing limits and end-stage renal disease may make use not recommended.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Baseline cardiac assessment: personal and family history of sudden death or ventricular arrhythmia; ECG if indicated by history/exam
Blood pressure and heart rate: baseline, after dose changes, and periodically during treatment
Weight and appetite: baseline and routinely (adults); height/weight growth tracking in children and adolescents
Sleep: onset insomnia, shortened sleep duration, delayed bedtime, and rebound sleepiness; adjust timing/formulation accordingly
Mood and behavior: irritability, anxiety, emotional lability; screen for depression and suicidality when clinically indicated
Psychosis/mania monitoring: new hallucinations, paranoia, delusions, or manic escalation; screen for bipolar risk before starting
Substance use risk: assess before prescribing and monitor throughout (early refills, dose escalation, lost prescriptions, multiple prescribers, non-oral routes)
Peripheral vasculopathy: cold/painful/color-changing digits; evaluate persistent symptoms and reduce dose or discontinue if needed
Tics/Tourette symptoms: assess history before starting; monitor for tic worsening during treatment

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Formulation choice is a big part of tolerability. Shorter coverage can mean less insomnia but more ups/downs. Longer coverage can feel smoother but can outlast your day if you’re sensitive.
items: Immediate-release tablets (Adderall and generics): 5 mg, 7.5 mg, 10 mg, 12.5 mg, 15 mg, 20 mg, 30 mg
Extended-release capsules (Adderall XR and generics): 5 mg, 10 mg, 15 mg, 20 mg, 25 mg, 30 mg
Triple-bead extended-release capsules (some generics/brands): 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 37.5 mg, 50 mg
Mydayis extended-release capsules: 12.5 mg, 25 mg, 37.5 mg, 50 mg
Administration option for some ER capsules: swallow whole or open and sprinkle beads on applesauce and consume immediately (do not chew; do not divide the capsule contents)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Amphetamines boost catecholamine signaling—mainly dopamine and norepinephrine—by increasing their release and reducing reuptake. In ADHD terms: they help the brain’s attention and self-regulation circuits stay online longer, so focus, planning, and impulse control require less brute force.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: For ADHD, stimulants are commonly first-line because the benefits can be fast and meaningful. The trade-off is tolerability and risk management: appetite, sleep, anxiety/irritability, cardiovascular monitoring, and misuse risk. If you have significant anxiety, bipolar disorder risk, psychosis history, active substance use, or cardiac disease, the decision is more nuanced and sometimes an alternative (non-stimulant ADHD meds and behavioral strategies) fits better.

seo.title: Dextroamphetamine/Amphetamine (Adderall): Uses, Dosage, Side Effects & Safety
seo.description: Adderall, Adderall XR, and Mydayis for ADHD (and IR for narcolepsy): dosing basics, how long it lasts, common side effects (sleep/appetite/anxiety), boxed warning on misuse/addiction, psychosis/mania risk, and key interactions.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Adderall-type mixed amphetamine salts are primarily used for ADHD. The goal is better attention, task initiation, follow-through, and impulse control—without feeling overstimulated. Immediate-release Adderall is also FDA-approved for narcolepsy-related daytime sleepiness.

Immediate-release (IR) commonly lasts 4-6 hours. Adderall XR often lasts 8-12 hours. Mydayis can last up to about 16 hours. Your actual duration depends on metabolism, dose, sleep, food, and whether you’re taking other meds that affect clearance.

faqs.q: Will Adderall make my anxiety worse?
faqs.a: It can. Stimulants may increase physical anxiety (jitteriness, faster heart rate) and irritability—especially at higher doses, with poor sleep, or with caffeine stacking. If anxiety ramps up, the fix is usually a dosing/timing/formulation adjustment (and treating underlying anxiety), not simply pushing through.

faqs.q: Why do stimulants cause appetite loss and weight loss?
faqs.a: They commonly reduce appetite and can delay hunger cues, so people unintentionally eat less. In kids, long-term appetite suppression can affect growth, which is why height/weight monitoring is part of standard care.

faqs.q: What’s the July 2025 FDA safety update about extended-release stimulants in kids under 6?
faqs.a: The FDA reported that children younger than 6 taking extended-release stimulants (including amphetamine- and methylphenidate-based ER products) can have higher drug exposure in the body and higher rates of side effects than older children—including clinically significant weight loss (≥10%). Labeling is being updated to reflect this. If a child under 6 is having weight loss or other adverse reactions on an extended-release stimulant, clinicians should consider stopping it and/or switching to an alternative (like an immediate-release option).

It can be. Adderall is Schedule II because it has high misuse potential. Misuse can lead to substance use disorder, overdose, and death—especially with higher doses or non-oral routes. Even when taken as prescribed, your clinician should monitor for misuse signals and keep the plan honest and safe.

faqs.q: Can I take Adderall with an SSRI or SNRI?
faqs.a: Sometimes, yes—but it needs monitoring. Combining stimulants with serotonergic meds can raise the risk of serotonin syndrome (rare, but serious), and some antidepressants can increase amphetamine exposure. If you’re on both, your prescriber should be thoughtful about dose, titration speed, and symptom monitoring.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between Adderall XR and Mydayis?
faqs.a: Both are extended-release amphetamine mixed salts, but their release designs and duration can differ. Adderall XR commonly covers 8-12 hours; Mydayis can last up to ~16 hours. The trade-off for longer coverage is often more insomnia risk if timing is off. They are not interchangeable mg-for-mg.

faqs.q: Can Adderall cause psychosis or mania?
faqs.a: Yes, in rare cases. Stimulants can trigger new psychotic symptoms (hallucinations, paranoia) or manic symptoms, especially in people with bipolar risk, psychosis history, or substance use vulnerability. If these symptoms appear, it’s urgent—contact your prescriber immediately and don’t keep taking it hoping it settles.

faqs.q: How do I stop Adderall safely?
faqs.a: If you’ve been taking it daily at steady doses, stopping suddenly can cause a crash—fatigue, low mood, irritability, and sleep changes. Many people do better with a gradual step-down plan. If you’re stopping because of severe side effects (psychosis/mania, major cardiovascular symptoms), your clinician may advise an immediate stop and urgent evaluation.

faqs.q: Why does it feel like it wears off and I crash?
faqs.a: Wearing off can bring rebound ADHD symptoms, fatigue, headache, or mood drop. This can improve with smoother extended-release coverage, better meal timing, hydration, sleep stabilization, or a medication schedule adjustment. If you’re crashing hard every day, that’s a solvable problem—not something you should just accept.
